title: Last rehearsal
brief: Write an original short story for an adult literary magazine's issue on rehearsals. A local radio drama is rehearsing with a stand-in sound-effects operator when one familiar sound no longer works. An actor and the stand-in have different ideas about whether the audience will notice. Let the work of making radio shape the action. Invent your own cast, setting, structure and ending. Submit a finished story, without an explanation or author bio.

# The Latch

The door was eleven inches wide and stood on the effects table between the gravel tray and the half coconut nobody had used since 1998. It had a brass knob, a frame of unpainted pine, and a thumb latch that for twenty-six years had made the sound of Dr. Aurelia Finch's surgery door closing on a patient. Now it made a sound like a spoon dropped in a drawer.

Petra worked it again. Clack. Something behind the plate had sheared, and the tongue no longer rode up the strike and fell. It just hit.

"That's not it," said Ines Varga, from the far side of the cast microphone, without lowering her script.

"No."

"Do it once more."

Petra did it once more. In the control room window Dov's head came up from the board. The talkback clicked. "What am I hearing?"

"The latch is gone," Petra said.

"Gone how?"

"Broken. Inside. I can open it up at the break."

"We have forty minutes of studio before the choir needs it for their thing. Keep going. Ines, from 'You'll want to keep that elevated.'"

They kept going. The show was *Marrow Road*, Thursday nights at seven-thirty on KVLT, a station whose signal covered two valleys and part of a third when the weather was right. It ran live from Studio B, which had been the Grange hall's cloakroom. Petra was a relief board operator who ran the overnight on weekends and had been asked nine days ago to do effects because Sol Brannigan had gone off a ladder cleaning his gutters and broken his wrist in two places. Sol had made the door. Sol had made most of the table. He had left her a cue script marked in three colors of pencil and a note that said *You'll be fine, don't let them rush the kettle.*

She was fine with the kettle. She was fine with footsteps on gravel, on boards, on the square of linoleum; she had learned to walk two shoes with her hands so that they sounded like a man with somewhere to be. She had the telephone bell and the cash drawer and the wet chamois in a bowl that was, in tonight's episode, a calf being born. She came in on the cue lights and got out clean.

"You'll want to keep that elevated," Ines said, in Dr. Finch's voice, which was lower than her own and unhurried. "And I'll want to see you Monday. Not Tuesday, Oskar. Monday."

"Monday," said Winston, who played Oskar Thule and four other men.

Footsteps, boards, going away. Petra walked the shoes off. Then the door. Clack.

Ines stopped. She didn't say anything this time. She only stopped, the way a person stops on a stair that isn't there, and the next line, which was hers, alone, to the empty surgery, went unsaid for three full seconds. Dov let the silence stand, then clicked in.

"Ines."

"I know. I'm sorry." She took off her glasses. She was sixty-eight and had been Dr. Finch since she was forty-two, since before the station had a website, since the show was recorded to tape in the mornings. "I can't play off that."

"It's a rehearsal."

"It's Thursday tomorrow."

"Petra will fix it at the break."

Petra said, "I'll look at it at the break."

Ines turned her head, and Petra understood the difference between those two sentences had been heard.

At the break she took the door into the corridor where the light was better and backed out the four screws with the driver on her knife. The spring was in two pieces. It was a flat leaf spring, bent to a shape nobody sold, blued and thin as a fingernail, and it had cracked across the bend, where it had flexed every Thursday since the first Bush administration. Sol had not bought this latch. He had taken it off something. There were older screw holes in the plate that didn't match the pine.

Ines came out with her tea. She looked at the parts laid on the windowsill.

"His mother's pantry," she said. "The house on Teller Street. He took it off the door the week they sold."

"I can't fix a spring like that. Not by tomorrow. Maybe not ever. I could bend something close out of a hacksaw blade but it'd take a few tries to get the temper."

"So what do we do?"

"There are two other latches in Sol's cabinet. One's a rim latch, heavier. And I can pull a door from the library, we've got about thirty."

"A recording."

"For one night."

"Of some other door."

Petra put the knife away. She had thought about how to say the next part, and had decided to say it flatly. "Nobody at home is going to know. It's a door closing. It's under a second long and it goes out through a compressor and a transmitter and comes out of a kitchen radio next to a running tap. I listened to the air checks. On air it's a thump with a little tick on the front."

"A tick and then a thump."

"On a good radio."

"That's what it is, though. The tick is the tongue going up. The thump is it coming down." Ines set her tea on the sill, beside the spring. "You think I'm being precious."

"I think you've heard it from four feet away for twenty-six years and they've heard it from across a room."

"Every week, though. Some of them every week since the start." She wasn't arguing hard; she seemed to be working it out as she went. "I get letters. Fewer now. A woman in Pruett wrote to say she shells peas to us. A man used to write who drove a milk tanker, he'd time his route so he was on the flat stretch by the reservoir where we come in clear. Do you know how every one of those scenes ends, the surgery scenes? Somebody leaves, and the door goes, and then I say something to nobody. That's the part people quote back to me. The line after the door. They never mention the door."

"Then they won't mention it tomorrow."

"No," Ines said. "They won't know what to mention. They'll just think I was a bit off."

Winston put his head around the corner. "Dov says two minutes, and he says he doesn't care if it's a mousetrap as long as it's on the light."

Petra screwed the plate back on over nothing, so it wouldn't rattle, and went to the cabinet.

They ran the scene with the rim latch. It was a good sound, to be fair to it; it had weight, and a little ring after. Ines said her line to the empty surgery and it came out as a line said to a studio. She shook her head before Dov could speak.

"It's a different house," she said. "That's a front door. That's a door with weather on the other side of it."

They ran it with the library. Dov fired it from the control room, a clean interior door, and it came down the monitor into the studio perfectly, and Ines missed it altogether, because there was nothing on the table for her to hear with the side of her face. She came in late and flat.

"I can't see you do it," she said to Petra, apologetically. "I never look. But I can't see you do it."

Dov clicked in. "Twenty-two minutes, friends."

Petra stood with her hands on the table. Her view had not changed: no pea-sheller in Pruett would tell one door from another through a five-inch speaker. But she had been watching the cue light and the script for nine days and now she'd been made to watch the actor. The door was a cue. Petra had been thinking of it as a thing sent out to the audience, and it was that, a little. Mostly it was a thing handed across the room to Ines, who then sent something out herself. The audience got the door secondhand, in the line.

So it didn't have to fool the valleys. It had to fool one woman four feet away, which was much harder.

"Give me a minute," she said. "Winston, talk to her about something."

She took the broken door and tried it with her eyes shut. Clack: the tongue hitting dead. The thump was still there, in a way; the pine frame still spoke when the little door met it. What was missing was the front. The tick. Up and over.

She tried a ballpoint, clicked just ahead. Too bright, a toy. She tried the cash drawer's catch, which was too long. She tried flicking the dead tongue with her thumbnail as she closed the door and got something tinny and late. Sol's cabinet had a cigar box of orphaned hardware and she went through it by ear, tapping things on the brass plate: a cupboard catch, a hasp, a skeleton key. The key was close. The key laid flat against the strike and tipped off it with one finger as the door came home gave a small bright step and then the wood.

"Try this," she said. "Don't look."

"I never look."

"From 'Monday.'"

"Not Tuesday, Oskar. Monday."

"Monday."

Shoes, boards, away. Key and door.

Ines waited. Everyone watched her wait. "Nearly," she said. "The thump's thin. It used to have a floor in it."

"The spring threw the tongue down. It hit harder." Petra looked around the table. She set the door frame on the square of linoleum, then took it off and set it on the footstep boards instead, the hollow box Sol had built for porches. "Again."

Key, door, and under it the box, answering.

Ines said, to the empty surgery, in the low unhurried voice, "Well. He won't come Monday."

It was the line as Petra had heard it on the air checks, the one that sounded like a woman alone, talking over her shoulder while she ran the tap. Winston grinned at the floor. In the window Dov had both hands raised like a man at a holdup.

"That's it?" Petra said.

"It's a quarter inch off," said Ines. "Do it exactly like that."

"I'm not sure I can do it exactly like that. It's three things with two hands."

"Then do it nearly like that every time, and I'll meet you." She put her glasses back on. "Sol was never exact either. He'd deny it."

They ran the scene twice more and the whole back half once, calf and all, and gave the room to the choir with a minute in hand. Petra taped the key to the door frame so it couldn't wander off and wrote on Sol's cue script, in a fourth color, *key flat on strike, tip w/ index, frame on porch box.* Then she put the two pieces of the spring in an envelope and wrote his name on it, because he would want them, and because he might know where there was another pantry.

On Thursday at seven fifty-one the light came on red, then her cue light, white. Oskar Thule's boots went away across the boards. Petra tipped the key and closed the door, and four feet off Ines drew a breath.

89b844eb3e059165.text:
The Second Fare

On the first run, when Ada put a nickel through the fare box, it sounded as if somebody had dropped a shirt button into a cup.

“Thank you, sir,” said Ruth, who had to say it whatever the man had paid with. On the other side of the glass, Lewis drew a finger across his throat. The red bulb went dark. Nobody took off their coats. The room where WMMT did its plays had once been the chilled part of a butcher shop, and in February the heat came on according to a principle known only to the butcher.

“They’ll notice,” Ruth said.

“They’ll hear a nickel go in,” Ada said. “What else do they need?”

Ada was covering for her brother Mickey, who had caught his hand in a sash window the previous Sunday. He had left her four pages of instructions. For the streetcar he had put simply, *Use box*. She had done the conductor’s steps with half soles on a piece of oak, the door with a folding toast rack, and the passage over the switch at Mercy Street by running two egg whisks briefly against each other. Lewis had let all that go by.

“The little bell comes after,” Ruth said.

“I know what it used to do.”

“There’s a man at the other end of the line who waits up Thursdays to hear that sound.”

“Is there?”

“I lived with him thirty-one years.”

Lewis came in from the control room. He put his hand into the fare box up to the wrist, as if the little bell might have come off in there. He tipped it toward the light, then gave Ada back her nickel. “You’ve got until eight-fifteen. I promised the farm bureau we’d give them the room at half past. Their poultry man has to get home.”

The play was called *Exact Change*. Ruth played a conductor on the last car of the night. A young man rode with her to the end of the line in order to pay a fare he had beaten as a boy. The car went out of service in the morning. They had been rehearsing since six, and it had been evident since about six-oh-five that the poor fellow was going to confess something worse if given any encouragement. He was played by a high school English teacher named Bill who had brought a covered dish to be collected by his wife. Whenever he said, “I owe this city something,” there came up through the holes in the lid a distinct smell of cabbage.

Ada turned the box upside down over a folded towel. Three Canadian pennies fell out, and a brass upholstery tack. Farther up she found a lever no longer attached to anything. The nickel used to tip the lever, which threw a little hammer against a bell. The hammer was gone.

“Probably Mickey’s got it in his pants,” she said. Mickey brought things home in his pockets to solder after supper. When his first child was born, he’d had to hand over six screws and a bicycle valve before the nurse would let him hold her.

“Mickey fixes it after,” Ruth said. “How are you going to do it now?”

Ada looked at the clock. “You could let the man ride free.”

“He’s been riding free forty years. That’s the play.”

They tried the desk bell from reception, with Ada’s thumb laid against the dome to stop it ringing on. On the monitor it sounded like a sick person calling for assistance. They tried a teaspoon drawn along the teeth of a comb, which was Lewis’s contribution and did nothing for anybody. Then Bill found two small wrenches in the bottom drawer. He held one by a length of string while Ada struck it with the other. Ruth sat with her back to them. She said it was close.

“Close in what sense?” Ada asked.

“In the sense that I can tell a man is trying to make a bell.”

Bill put the wrenches back. “My wife can generally tell when I’m trying, too.” He checked the lid of the dish and returned to his mark, the white cross where he stood for his scenes inside the car.

Ruth was studying her script, a pencil stuck lengthwise into the waves above her ear. She had done a conductor’s run herself during the war. Ada knew it because she had seen a photograph in the station lobby, a row of women in uniform standing with their hands behind them, Ruth at the end with the point of somebody else’s elbow in her side. In the first scene she had corrected Bill about the way he got on. He was coming up too fast for the height of the step. Bill, who was six foot four, had obligingly got off again.

“Do you ever listen to this program at home?” Ada asked.

“I work here Thursdays.”

“I mean on a set. You want to hear what comes out of ours. You could fry an egg in the middle of a love scene and my mother would think they’d started kissing.”

Ruth took the pencil out of her hair. “You think people listen badly because they own cheap radios?”

“I think my mother owns a cheap radio.”

Through the glass Lewis held up five fingers, meaning the last five pages. They would come back to the opening. Ada got the car under way with a sewing machine motor under the table. At low speed the belt had an uneven pull that gave the car an agreeable load of passengers, though the only ones in the script were Bill and a drunk asleep behind him. On page nineteen the drunk woke up and got off. Ada took her foot a little off the pedal and the car went easier. She saw Ruth glance her way.

At the end of the line, Bill confessed to having watched another boy put off the car for the fare he himself had beaten. Rain in the gutters, running feet, the other boy’s face at the glass. Ruth let a second pass after his speech. The space she left was so exactly the space in which a conductor might decide she had been told worse things that Ada nearly missed the brake.

“Pay it, then,” Ruth said.

Ada dropped the nickel.

“That’s one,” Ruth said. “Now who’s going to pay for him?”

That was the last line. The script called for the little bell a second time, then music. Ada had to fish the nickel out again. While she was doing it, somebody in the corridor lifted the lid on Bill’s cabbage and replaced it very quietly.

Lewis came out. “You really need two nickels.”

“You really need a second customer,” Bill said. “Who pays the other fare?”

“I do,” Ruth said.

“On a conductor’s wages?”

“It’s my last day. I can go crazy.”

Ada set the nickel on the towel. “That’s why you want the bell. You don’t think they’ll know she paid.”

Ruth undid the top button on her coat at last. Underneath it she wore the blue wool uniform from the photograph. The shoulders had gone shiny and there was a neat blue insert under each arm. “I’d like them to know *somebody* did.”

Ada went out to reception for change. At the front desk sat a red-haired woman with a ledger open before her, writing down the names of listeners who wanted the poultry booklet. Already she had a page and a half, though the poultry man was still in the hall eating cabbage. At Ada’s request she opened the till. She gave her two nickels for a dime and asked what they were doing back there.

“Streetcar play.”

“Is Ruth in it?”

“Yes.”

“My dad used to take us down to ride her car. We could’ve walked wherever we went. We’d wait for hers.”

“What did the fare box sound like?”

The woman considered. “I don’t know. We were little. Dad paid.”

On her way back Ada stopped at the water fountain. From inside the studio she could hear Ruth saying her last line to Bill again, giving the weight to *him* this time. Outside the door it sounded mean. She said it once more, in a lower voice, and Ada heard, for the first time, the invitation in it. Bill apparently heard it too. There was a rattle of change, then Ruth laughed.

Ada went back in. “Let me do one with you,” she said.

She moved the box from the effects table to a chair beside Ruth’s microphone. She gave Bill a nickel and put the other in Ruth’s hand. Lewis, at the board again, made a turning motion for them to hurry up.

“From ‘Pay it, then,’” Ada said. “Do what you’d do if you had the money.”

Bill dropped his coin and Ruth asked who was going to pay for the boy. There was a small sound quite far down, then the second coin fell. Lewis kept the red light on through a good six seconds of wool rubbing against wool and Bill breathing through his nose. Then he played it back.

The small sound had been Ruth undoing the clasp of her change purse. She’d put the nickel away as soon as Ada had given it to her. Heard on the monitor, it was a dry double click, intimate as somebody taking out her teeth beside you in bed. After it came the blunt knock of the fare. You could hear whose money it was. You could hear what it cost her to have Bill stand and watch her get it out.

“Again,” Ruth said.

They went from the top. At the first fare Ada used the box on the chair and kept the motor running, so the nickel went in under the hum. Near the end she let the car run down until all you could hear was the belt making its last trip around. Bill told his story into the quiet. This time, when Ruth opened her purse, he turned his head a little from the microphone. It sounded as if he’d had the decency to look away.

At eight twenty-seven Lewis let in the poultry man. Bill took his empty dish home. Ada was winding the motor cord around her hand when Ruth came over with the fare box tucked under one arm.

“So would he have noticed?” Ada asked.

“My husband? Inside of a minute.”

“What would he have said?”

“Nothing till the music was over. Then I’d have heard about it.”

Ruth worked the little lever through the slot with the point of her pencil. It swung freely, making no sound. “I used to know who needed help getting on just by how long it took between the step and the bell. Some nights you could get most of your supper eaten up front in the dark.”

She put the box down. Ada slipped the two nickels into the pocket of the uniform for Thursday. From the studio came the poultry man’s voice, full and round and perfectly at home in all the kitchens of the county. He was telling people how to candle an egg. Hold it up, he said, and give your eyes time.

Ruth picked up her coat and the coins touched through the blue wool. Both women turned their heads.

63e6f7a33e42c198.text:
The first time Ruth said, “You can let yourself out,” nobody moved. Ellis had already left the microphone. He stood at the end of the carpet with his script rolled against his thigh. At the effects table, Nina lifted the brass latch and tried it again.

There was a faint tick.

“That’s it?” Ruth asked.

“It goes down,” Nina said. “It just doesn’t come back.”

She held up the little board on which the latch was mounted. A spring had broken inside the casing. She had found half of it in the bottom of the box, under two coconuts and a bag of aquarium gravel.

From the control room, Len said, “Take it from ‘You can.’”

“You can let yourself out,” Ruth said.

Nina pushed the latch up with her thumb, then let it fall. A tick and a clack, with a small interval between.

“Good enough,” Len said.

“Other way round,” Ruth said.

Nina looked at her.

“There’s a clack when you lift it and a tick when it catches. That one sounds like somebody locking a suitcase.”

Nina set the board down gently, which made a third sound, a hollow wooden knock. “How many people do you think could tell you what that latch sounds like?”

“None of them.”

“All right.”

“They’ll still know.”

Through the glass Len showed them five fingers. It was six minutes past seven. At half past, the station went live to the school board meeting, and the studio had to be empty. Tonight they were rehearsing in the clothes they’d come in, parkas over chair backs, a grocery bag under Ruth’s music stand with a tub of yogurt going soft inside it. The following night was the broadcast. Nina, who normally read the school lunch menus and recorded the notices for the animal shelter, was filling in for Bert. He’d had the cataract in his right eye done on Monday. He had left her a page of instructions, including a sketch of where to put the microphone for the grapefruit crossing the kitchen floor. About the latch he had written DOOR.

The serial had been on Thursday nights for eleven years. Ruth played Iona, who let rooms over a hardware store. Learners of English called the station sometimes to ask what Iona had said. People who had grown up in town called to correct the prices. A man who plowed the county roads once sent in a drawing of the building, showing the stairs on the outside, and Ruth had turned it over on the table and drawn the stairs on the inside. She had never asked Len which drawing he kept.

Nina turned to the script. “Could we have him go on ‘out’? I can get his steps clean if he starts there.”

“He waits for the latch.”

“Why?”

“He’s waiting for her to open it for him.”

Nina looked from Ruth to Ellis. He had unrolled his script. He was twenty-three and played a man of thirty-seven. When he needed to be tired, he bent his knees.

“I thought I opened it myself,” he said.

“You do, eventually.”

“Have we been doing that the whole time?”

“Every time you leave angry.”

Len’s talkback clicked. “Let’s hear the eventually.”

Ellis returned to the microphone. In the scene he had come to get a reference from Iona. He had lived upstairs for eight years, and now he wanted a place with a yard, even though he had no children and was allergic to grass. Iona had written that he always paid in cash. The prospective landlord wanted to know if he was dependable.

“You could say I was quiet,” Ellis read.

“I could say you had good curtains.”

“They were there when I moved in.”

“Yes,” Ruth said. The word was meant to sound as though Iona had enjoyed something without knowing it until now. That had come easily in Ruth’s kitchen that morning. In the studio, she could hear herself trying to be pleased.

Ellis folded the reference. The paper by his microphone was a sheet of brown wrapping cut down to letter size. Ordinary paper had vanished in the mix when they first tried it.

“You can let yourself out,” Ruth said.

She heard him draw in breath for a line he didn’t have. It was an excellent breath. There was room in it for a person to reconsider. Then there was room for the latch, and after that there was just room.

“Walking,” Len said through the speaker.

Ellis started across the carpet. Nina took two steps in Bert’s box of linoleum, missed the third because she was watching Ellis, and produced the fourth after he’d stopped.

Ruth laughed. She couldn’t help it. It sounded as if he’d left the building and come back for his hat.

Nina took her foot out of the box. “I could do it if everybody stood still.”

Ellis went back to his mark.

“I mean you, too,” Nina said to Ruth. “Every time he goes, you turn your page.”

Ruth looked down. Her thumb was under the corner. The next scene took place three weeks later and began with Iona peeling an orange. The script said nothing about what she did after the man left. Ruth always turned there, taking care to lift the sheet by the edge so it wouldn’t drag across the stand.

Len came in for the latch. He shook it beside his ear. “Bert might have another one.”

“He said there’s only that one,” Nina said.

“When did you talk to Bert?”

“Last night. He asked me to read him the script. He wanted to know if the man took the reference.”

“Does he?” Ellis asked.

Ruth pointed to the sheet of wrapping paper in his hand.

“I could leave it,” he said.

“Then what are you going to show the landlord?”

“I thought he’d already seen it.”

There had been seven episodes about the reference. In one, Iona had gone downstairs to the hardware store to borrow a pen. In another, the man had brought up a bowl of plums to show that he was in no particular hurry. Ruth could remember who had played the shop assistant when they’d gone down for the pen, and the noise of the stone Bert had sucked clean for the last plum. She couldn’t remember whether the landlord had seen the letter. Len took off his glasses. They had four minutes.

Nina went to the studio door and pressed down the handle. It let out a nylon squeak. Beyond it, two folding chairs waited by the drinking fountain for members of the public to come in and speak at the school board meeting. The board members were meeting across town. Anybody who didn’t have a phone could make a comment from the studio.

“No,” Ruth said.

“I’m getting my bag.”

Nina brought in a canvas bag with a broken zipper, reached into it, and drew out a spoon. She tried the bowl of it against the iron microphone base. Too high. She laid the spoon flat against the latch board and slid it off the edge.

Ruth raised her head.

“Do it again,” she said.

Nina did. There was a scrape followed by a little jump in the wood as the bowl passed the edge. It was close enough that Ruth felt her own wrist turn. Nina took a nail from the effects box and tapped it once against the back of the spoon. That supplied the catch.

“Now if I could do that with my feet,” she said.

Len went back to the booth. Ruth took the spoon. It was warm from Nina’s hand. Nina showed her where to start, with the spoon almost off the board, and how lightly the nail had to touch. They moved the effects microphone nearer the music stand, and Len asked Ruth for a line to check the spill.

“You can let yourself out,” she said.

Something in the speaker popped.

“Again. Look where you were looking before.”

She had been looking at Ellis. She looked at him now and found him studying the reference, though there was nothing on it but the blue smudge that told them which side was quieter. He could see the smudge from where he held the paper. He turned it over as if he expected something on the other side.

“You can let yourself out,” Ruth said.

She lowered the spoon to the wood. Ellis didn’t move. When Bert did the latch he watched the script and took the gap every time. Ruth had thought of that gap as hers. Bert would be sitting at home tomorrow with his head tilted away from the radio to keep the sound on his good side. He would know how long she took, and whether she had meant to take that long.

Ellis lifted his eyes. He seemed about to fold the paper again, smaller this time. For a moment Ruth wanted him to put it down. She could have said something about the cash, about the trouble she’d gone to finding a pen. One of the plums had been split, and Iona had eaten that one first. Ruth moved her thumb. The spoon slid off the edge of the board.

At the far end of the studio, Nina took the first step. She took the second a little faster. Ruth tapped the nail, and Nina stopped with the sole of one shoe still making contact with the linoleum. She eased her weight onto it until the floor gave a tiny complaint. Then nothing. In the glass Ruth could see Len watching the second hand pass the top of the clock.

“Keep that,” he said, and dropped the talkback.

Ellis was still holding the reference. The board meeting music came up faintly through the wall. Out in the hall a woman took one of the folding chairs, keeping her coat on, and arranged a stack of papers in her lap. Nina crossed to the studio door to let her in. She had to lift the handle first and then pull it down, a thing everyone who worked at the station did by feel. Ruth heard the squeak she’d heard a few minutes earlier. Then the woman’s papers slid off her lap and fanned out on the floor.

Ellis laid the reference on the nearest chair and stooped to help. Nina held the door open with her heel. The woman gathered the pages as he handed them to her, turning each one right side up and checking the number at the bottom. Ruth stayed by the effects table. She put the nail back in the box and lifted the spoon to carry it to Nina. The bowl had left a clean stripe in the dust on the board. She set it down again, a little farther back, where tomorrow she could find the place with her thumb.
